<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par118 />the ''casus loci'' a termination ({{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}) is employed, in which (according to {{GHGpar|90|c}}) the old accusatival ending is preserved; and finally from the consistency with which classical Arabic puts these nearer definitions in the accusative (which may be recognized by its form) even under circumstances in which one would be rather inclined to expect a nominative in apposition.

{{GHGmargin-letter|118|c}}
The relation subsisting between the circumstantial accusative and the accusative of the object is especially apparent when the former (as e.g. in a statement of the goal after a verb of motion) is immediately connected with its verb. But even the more loosely connected circumstantial definitions are certainly to be regarded as originally objects of a governing word habitually omitted, only that the consciousness of this closer government was at length lost, and the accusative more and more acquired an independent value as a ''casus adverbialis''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|118|d}}
'''2.''' The accusative serves to define more precisely the ''place'' (''accus. loci''), either (''a'') in answer to the question ''whither?'' after verbs of motion,<ref>So commonly in Sanskrit; in Greek only poetically, e.g. Iliad i. 317 κνίση δ᾽ οὐρανὸν ἷκεν: in Latin, e.g. ''rus ire, Romam proficisci''.</ref> or (''b'') in answer to the question ''where?'' after verbs of ''being, dwelling, resting'', &c. (but also after transitive verbs, see the examples), or finally (''c'') to define more precisely the ''extent'' in space, in answer to the question ''how far? how high? how much?'', &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|118|e}}
Instead of the simple accusative, the locative (see above, {{GHGpar|90|c}})
<ref>Hence e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=26}} the Masora requires {{GHGheb|text=הַגָּ֫גָה}} instead of the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGheb|text=הַגָּג}}.</ref> is frequently found in the cases mentioned under ''f'' (sometimes also in those under ''g'') or the preposition {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}},<ref>So in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=18}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־בֵּית י׳}} the better reading is {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־בּ׳}}.</ref> especially before persons as the aim of the movement, or {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}, usually, to express being ''at'' a place.

{{GHGmargin-letter|118|f}}
Examples of (''a''): {{GHGheb|text=נֵצֵא הַשָּׂדֶה|translate=let us go out into the field}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=11}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=לָלֶ֫כֶת תַּרְשִׁישׁ|translate=to go to Tarshish}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=20|verse=36}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=27|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=11|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=8}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=134|verse=2}}; with {{GHGheb|text=לָקַח}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=14}}; with {{GHGheb|text=נָתַן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=24}}; with the ''accus. loci'' emphatically preceding (cf. Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=8}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=5|hidebook=1}}; with {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא}} (in the sense of ''aggredi'', equivalent to {{GHGheb|text=עַל־ בּוֹא}}, cf. {{GHGpar|117|a}}, note 2) the ''personal'' aim also is poetically added in the accusative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=32|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=38|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=10|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=28|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=22|hidebook=1}}; but in the last passage it is better taken as an accusative of the object (cf. the German ''einen ankommen, überkommen''). See also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=36}} (where {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב}} can hardly be transitive); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=20}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} has probably fallen out after {{GHGheb|text=ישראל}}; so Strack).—Finally, cf. also the use of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר ... שָׁ֫מָּה|translate=whither}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=13|verse=27}}.—The ''accus. loci'' occurs after a passive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=15}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|118|g}}
Examples of (''b''): {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=11}} ''remain a widow'' {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית אָבִיךְ}} ''in thy father’s house''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hos|chapter=12|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=6|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=33|verse=20}}; {{GHGheb|text=פֶּ֫תַח הָאֹ֫הֶל|translate=in the tent door}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=1}}, 10, 19:11, and frequently. As observed by Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=29}}, accusatives of this kind are almost without exception (but cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=33|verse=20}}) connected with a noun in the genitive. In all the above examples, however, the accusative may have been preferred to the natural construction with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} (which is not rare even with {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית}} and {{GHGheb|text=פֶ֫תַח}}) for euphonic reasons, in order to avoid the combination of such sounds as {{GHGheb|text=בְּב׳}} and {{GHGheb|text=בְּפ׳}}; cf., moreover, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=6|verse=8}} ({{GHGheb|text=הַמִּזְבֵּחַ}} instead of the usual {{GHGheb|text=הַמִּזְבֵּ֫חָה}}<section end=par118 /><noinclude>
